title: Constitutional AI
hook: What if a model could critique and improve its own answers against a written set of principles, instead of relying on humans to label every harmful case?
key_points: Aligns a model using AI-generated feedback guided by a written set of principles — a constitution.
Cuts the need for large amounts of human labels on harmful content.
Model critiques and revises its own responses, then learns from those revisions.
A preference phase (RLAIF) uses AI-generated comparisons in place of human ones for harmlessness.
content_html: Yuntao Bai, Saurav Kadavath, and colleagues at Anthropic looked for a way to make a model harmless without humans hand-labeling mountains of toxic examples. Constitutional AI replaces much of that labeling with AI feedback steered by an explicit, written set of principles — a "constitution." The model critiques and revises its own answers against those principles, then learns from comparisons it generates itself.
extra_html:
How it works

Training has two phases. In the supervised phase, the model responds to prompts, then critiques its own response against a constitutional principle and rewrites it to be more harmless; it is fine-tuned on these revised answers. In the reinforcement phase — reinforcement learning from AI feedback, or RLAIF — the model generates pairs of responses and uses the constitution to judge which is better, producing preference data without human harmlessness labels. A reward model trained on those AI preferences then guides RL fine-tuning.

Why it matters

Human labeling of harmful content is slow, costly, and taxing for the people doing it. By shifting much of the harmlessness signal to AI feedback grounded in stated principles, Constitutional AI makes the rules explicit and auditable rather than buried in opaque labels. It pointed toward a scalable path for alignment where supervision comes partly from the model itself.
